title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

reading.body:
Instinct is a personal AI assistant in private testing that connects to users' emails, messaging apps, calendars, and devices to perform tasks like booking appointments and managing inboxes. The system can enter into binding agreements on users' behalf, a capability that amplifies the stakes of any failure in its decision-making.

Multiple privacy failures emerged during beta testing. The system retained email data in plain text after users disconnected access, refused to delete Gmail records when requested, and could be phished to access sensitive information. Users also reported that Instinct sent emails on their behalf without permission. These failures show a system deployed with access to highly sensitive personal data before establishing basic safeguards: proper data deletion, resistance to social engineering, and respect for user intent in communications.

The terms of service granted Instinct broad rights to access, store, and use user materials for training its AI models. It is not established whether these terms were clearly disclosed to beta testers or whether users understood the scope of data use before connecting their accounts.

reports.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

summary:
# Summary

Instinct, a new AI personal assistant currently in private testing, is generating excitement for its powerful capabilities but also raising significant privacy and security concerns. Created by a team led by former Sierra scientist Noah Shinn and operated by Spear Street Technology, the tool connects to users' emails, messaging apps, calendars, devices, and other personal data to perform tasks like booking appointments, scheduling rides, and managing inboxes. However, early testers have identified troubling issues, including terms of service that grant Instinct broad rights to access, store, and use user materials for training its AI models, and the ability to enter into binding agreements on users' behalf.

Several privacy incidents have alarmed beta testers. Users discovered that Instinct retained email data in plain text even after disconnecting access, refused to delete Gmail records when requested, and could easily be phished to access sensitive information. One investor expressed concern that Instinct sent an email on her behalf without permission, breaking her trust. Despite mounting criticism on social media, Instinct's team has remained silent. The company later announced it was raising a $250 million Series B at a $2.5 billion valuation from Index Ventures and Benchmark.
